text:
***** Read that again. 
"You think an almost 2 year old card that was barely high end then, should still be as fast as top of the mid tier?"

The 970 was barely top tier, I said the 480 is top of the MID tier now. It's a mid ranged GPU, of course, but the 470, GTX 1050 and 1060 will be mid tier GPUs too, and of course 470x, 480x, 1050Ti, 1060Ti, any of those will be mid tier if we see any of them release(might not obviously).

I'm not saying the 480 is bad or anything, it's just not impressive, it performs as should've been expected considering the last couple of years in GPU performance, like 290x=390=480. 780=970=1060(probably). With the huge die shrink and all the hype behind these releases, and the 1070 being 980ti performance(very impressive, although the price of the 1070 is too high for a 70 series GPU), I honestly thought the 480 would be better.

As for crossfire, 480=390. XFire 390s trade blows with a single 980Ti. If a game scales well with XFire, the 390s would win. However, a single faster GPU is almost always the better choice. And since 480=390, 1070=980Ti, the 1070 is a better option than XFire 480s. It's also like $50-$100 cheaper for a 1070 than XFire 480s.

I don't care about NVidia as a company, if they're shitty or not, all I care about is performance. I'll stick with my 970 that performs on par with a 480 and has less FPS drops, and drops to lower FPS when it DOES drop. Obviously though, buying new, 480 makes sense, even if it's around the same price as the 970 but if a new 970 is a good bit cheaper than a new 480, I'd go with the 970 for sure.

I just really want AMD and NVidia to step their god damned game up big time, which neither of them really have. 

Maybe the GTX 1060 will be nice, it could be GTX 980/390x performance for the same price as a 480, which could be very nice. Or NVidia could totally fuck up, and be like 380x performance. It's hard to tell because the GTX 960 was terrible, but the 1070 is a really good card at an exceptional price for it's performance, it's just over-priced for a 70 series GPU.

text:
I'm very interested in seeing how this compares to other cards at 4K with only FXAA or other AA's with very low performance impact.

I say that because I've been able to run a R9 280x at 4K (AMH 399u) in games like Crysis 3, Project Cars, and Tomb Raider with a mix of ultra, high, and a little medium while turning down the "filters" to just FXAA. And with that i would get about 50fps-60fps making sure i don't see 45fps often at all (v-sync off). Honestly I've always thought FXAA made games look very bad at 1080p as it tends to distort edges very badly to the point that you can't see enemies through grass, but not in 4K as the edge blurring is 4 times smaller and thus not nearly as distracting if at all. In fact during gameplay it's almost indistinguishable from MSAA in 4K, but of course if you take a screenshot MSAA will look much nicer. And the other way around with other AA's at 1080p as i would always jack up MSAA to 8x and others the same. FYI, hate motion blur.

the extra 4 GB of memory does make a difference because textures, shadows and your other graphical settings take up video memory. If you want to play at the highest settings in some games, it will sometimes push a bit over the 4GB mark which means that the 4GB version can't get the highest settings in some games but the 8GB version can because it has alot more video memory. Though there is a problem here, i don't think the RX 480 is fast enough in it's current state to utilize all of 8GB efficiently, but don't worry about that, overclocking the card should fix that.

text:
For anyone disappointed(stop listening to hype) or complaining of performance: 

The RX 480's die is 232mm², R9 390's die is 438mm², and the 970's die is 398mm². Stop complaining about small performance increase when the increase is there in the die size, performance/watt, and performance/price. The RX 480's die size is similar to the size of a R7 370 which is 212mm² and the GTX 950/960's die size which is 227mm².  So this gpu on a die size level is replacing cards of much lower tiers with much better performance. Considering this card is replacing the 380/380x in their lineup (both cards 359mm² die size) then this card is quite impressive.

text:
I don't understand the people saying this is disappointing. Do you not realise the difference between reference cards(Generally the worse performing forms of the cards) and custom cards? Practically all cards that aren't reference get a lot of tweeks to improve power consumption, overclocking capability and lower heat generated. The 970 SuperSC by EVGA is their top tier OCed GPU(Behind FTW OC versions) while it's being compared to a reference RX 480 and a barely OCed MSI R9 390, which is only overclocked by around 20Mhz, where the 970 SSC is OCed by 140Mhz out of the box. It's comparing a card at the brink of it's safe max performance to a card that isn't being brought to that point in the slightest while the RX 480 and R9 390 are still on par or outperforming the 970 in practically every game(With more VRAM).

The price for the RX 480 should be comparable to a 960 which is around €260 right now for R9 390 and OC'ed 970 performance with the headroom of full 4GB VRAM or 8GB VRAM. When this card gets the custom treatment from MSI, ASUS and the likes you're going to see the RX 480 outperform the R9 390 and the 970. Right now the 970 and R9 390s are €100 more expensive than a 960 or 380/380X which makes the RX 480 the card to get if you're looking for a card in that price range especially if you can wait a month or two for better performance, better cooling and higher grade materials used from MSI or ASUS.

There is literally no reason to buy an R9 390 right now with the RX 480 unless you already have one and want to CF. There's even less of a reason to get any 970 due to the VRAM limitations alone plus the fact the card has to be seriously overclocked to make it comparable to R9 390 performance.

The RX 480 is the best bang for your buck. If you're looking from an upgrade from a mid-tier card the RX 480 is definitely the card to get.

This simply isn't true. Manual OCing has resulted in at least +200Mhz core clock and +7Mhz memory OC on the R9 390.

Even at that JayZTwoCents has manually OCed both the 970 and R9 390 and found the R9 390 was still faster than the 970 when both were manually OCed.

Then you also have to remember that they're two different cards. While one card can reach, say, 100Mhz or even 200Mhz higher OC than another card(or 970 vs a 390), it does not make it faster than the card with lesser Mhz to OC. The difference is only in performance. The OC value is in how much you can push out of the card so in a OC vs OC review the R9 390 will trump the 970 regardless. The only difference is reviewers can only get their hands on vastly OCed 970s(Which, on a consumer level, equates to more costly GPUs for the privilege of having it OCed out of the box) to compare to 390s that are hardly OCed at all unless they opt to manually overclock them.

text:
Raisin Toast you need to take into consideration that more games are going to be made with next gen api's, and the scaling works alot better and can even cross vendor, the reason why current dx11/dx9 games is because of how high level they are, the encoding needed to activate them wasn't worth the hassle, now because how low level dx12's coding is, it is soo much easier to access stuff on there, the erraticness is going to drop with multi gpu setups. just remember the 480 is designed as an entry to medium level card, alot of pc building companies may change to the 480 4GB as their cheap prebuilt pc gpu which will let them tot it as entry level VR pc and able to charge a little more, which is going to help AMD take a fair chunk of the market if Nvidia don't get their finger out and release 1050/1060.

heavyweight you misunderstand the gpu scaling in dx12, the reason gpu's hit 100% load on both during dx9/dx11 games was due to the api making each gpu produce the frame that came after the other one, therefore they were both rendering full screens 1 frame apart, where as in dx12 it is focused on halving the load, so each gpu is making half the screen so the amount of actual rendering each gpu is doing per frame is halved, which is why if you watched some of the videos you would notice that in dual gpu the power draw wasn't exactly doubled like it used to be.

text:
+beretta9m2f 
Assuming the data on gpu-z is somewhat correct, your conclusion, is incorrect. A thing to note here: NVidia's SLI is different from AMD's CF technology, so you can't compare them, in fact, comparing two gpus without actual data on how they work in games is wrong too, but until we see more elaborate benchmarks and comparisons, it'll have to do:

Links: 
https://www.techpowerup.com/gpudb/2839/geforce-gtx-1080
https://www.techpowerup.com/gpudb/2848/radeon-rx-480

Math time ;)
A GTX1080 has 8,228 GFLOPS and 257.1 GTexel/s, an RX480 has 5,834 GFLOPS and 182.3 GTexel/s , now, i think we can all agree that CF and SLI aren't perfect technologies, so they won't achieve 100% efficiency, but, let's say that the efficiency of both of the RX480s drops to around 80% when they are connected, this means that they will have :
5834 * 2*0.8=9334 GFLOPS Higher than the GTX1080.
182.3*2*0.8=291.2 GTexel/s Again, higher than the GTX1080.

From these, you can say that two 480s will outperform a 1080, obviously, driver and game optimizations are neglected here, but nevertheless, the numbers don't lie.
PS: With 70% CF efficiency two rx 480s would have 8167 GFLOPS and 255.2 GTexel/s , very close to the GTX1080, but i do believe CF has an efficiency of around 80%.

Feel free to correct me on this. Oh, in 2009 CF efficiency was around 50-70% so i'd think they got to 80% by now, i mean, 7 years...

PPS: I believe CF works by having the firs card at 100% Efficiency and then the second card at 80% efficiency, or whatever, but this comment is for comparative purposes, not exact performance deductions.

text: Damon Llopiz Well, I did a bit of research, and I am calling baloney on the point you made. Anyone who is buying a graphics card would be foolish to use power draw as a comparable statistic. A person would have bigger things to worry about if their house could not handle drawing 500 watts from a PC. Heck, the average microwave draws anywhere from 500-1000 watts during heating! Additionally, there are plenty of graphics cards out for sale that have a similar price per watt. For example, the r9 285 comes in at $1.37/watt compared to the rx 480's $1.33/watt. Performance per watt or even price to performance ratio is a better comparison. Even then, the 1070 has around twice the performance for twice the price, hence all the videos comparing the two lately. In conclusion, while the 480 is indisputably a very well priced mid to low end card, there is no grounds to argue that it is anywhere near competitive with ANY current gen cards. I would consider it another choice in the lineup of new cards this year, but not superior or comparable to them, just like you would not argue that a 1070 is better than a 1080.
